S18.title: Pineapple Leaf Wilt Disease (Roboflow dataset page)

classes.explanation: This label comes from the image dataset the model was trained on. We could not find an established pineapple disease called 'leaf blight' in the Indian official IPM package, so treat this result as 'a leaf-lesion pattern that resembles the dataset's blight images', not as a confirmed named disease.

symptoms.text: Documented pineapple leaf-spot diseases include white leaf spot: small brown spots at rubbed leaf margins that lengthen in wet weather and dry to papery cream or white patches with brown margins.
Other regional reports describe leaf spots with banded light-brown to reddish-brown edges that can merge into large lesions (Exserohilum rostratum, Hainan; Penicillium oxalicum, Leizhou).
A student thesis describes Curvularia leaf spot starting as small yellow-brown spots that enlarge to dark brown irregular patches.

look_alikes.text: Nutrient deficiency, sunscald, mechanical rubbing damage and mite damage can resemble disease; NIPHM notes that unclear symptoms need close examination or lab analysis.
Early mealybug wilt can show reddish leaves and leaf-tip death.

immediate_actions.text: Examine several leaves and neighbouring plants; record percent of leaf area affected and how many plants show it.
Collect and destroy badly diseased leaves and plant debris; keep field drained.

non_chemical.text: Remove and destroy diseased plant parts and crop residues; use healthy planting material; maintain drainage; weekly field monitoring.

chemical_control.message: No verified chemical-control recommendation is available in the current knowledge base for this crop, condition, and location. Consult a qualified agricultural extension officer before applying pesticides.
chemical_control.reason: Kerala university and older national pages list fungicides, but none was verified as a current registered pineapple label for this condition and location.

prevention.text: Avoid wounding leaves during field operations; use sterilised tools; avoid planting in wet weather.
prevention.note: Wound-entry is documented for white leaf spot and butt rot; assumed relevant to other leaf spots, unconfirmed.

spread_reduction.text: Destroy infected debris away from the field; avoid moving plant parts between plots.

monitoring.text: Scout weekly; re-photograph the same leaf after a set interval to see whether lesions are spreading.
monitoring.note: Weekly interval is from NIPHM general scouting; photo re-check is an app design choice.

seek_expert_help: Spots are spreading across many plants or leaves.
Cause is unclear or the result conflicts with what you see.
classes.geographic_applicability: No Manipur- or NE-India-specific source found. Regional reports are from China, Indonesia and Kerala.
unresolved: Which pathogen(s) the dataset's 'blight' images represent is not documented in the sources we could access.
No source ties the label to a specific management protocol.

classes.explanation: Fusarium diseases of pineapple are best documented on fruit and stems. Leaf-based identification of Fusarium is weakly supported in the literature we found, so this result is a visual resemblance only and cannot confirm the pathogen.

symptoms.text: Fusariosis is described as affecting all plant parts but most visible and damaging on fruit; stem girdling or killing can cause rosetting and curvature.
Fruitlet core rot shows as internal browning with no external signs on many fruit, so it cannot be seen on leaves.

look_alikes.text: Base (butt) rot, Phytophthora heart rot, nutrient problems and mealybug wilt can all produce wilting or discolouring leaves.

immediate_actions.text: Check the stem base and heart of the plant and, if fruiting, fruit; note any gum, rot, or stem distortion.
immediate_actions.note: Inspection steps adapted from NIPHM disease descriptions; not a protocol written for this class.

immediate_actions.text: Remove and destroy diseased plants and debris.

non_chemical.text: Use fresh, disease-free suckers/planting material; avoid wounding plants; handle fruit carefully; keep drainage good; collect and destroy debris.

chemical_control.message: No verified chemical-control recommendation is available in the current knowledge base for this crop, condition, and location. Consult a qualified agricultural extension officer before applying pesticides.
chemical_control.reason: No current registered pineapple fungicide label was located.

prevention.text: NIPHM states infection of flowers and fruit occurs mainly through insect injuries and infected planting material, so insect control and clean planting material matter.

spread_reduction.text: Do not move infected plant parts between fields; destroy rejected fruit and refuse.

monitoring.text: Weekly scouting of leaves, stems and, later, fruit.

seek_expert_help: Any suspected Fusarium case, since confirmation needs laboratory culture or molecular testing.
Rosetting, stem curvature or gummy fruit rot.
classes.geographic_applicability: NIPHM names F. guttiforme for India, but Jacobs et al. (2010) say fusariosis from F. guttiforme was reported only from South America; F. ananatum is the species found in South Africa, Costa Rica and elsewhere. Which Fusarium species occurs in Manipur is unresolved.
unresolved: Evidence that Fusarium produces a reliable visible leaf pattern is not established in the sources we read.
Species present in NE India unverified.
A 2020 Philippine paper appears to report Fusarium on pineapple leaves, but only a garbled excerpt was accessible, so it was not used.

classes.explanation: The model sees no pattern resembling the three disease classes in this photo. That does not prove the plant is healthy: roots, stem base, heart, fruit and insects such as mealybugs are not visible in a leaf photo.

look_alikes.text: Early mealybug wilt, root rots and nematode damage can occur before leaves look abnormal; NIPHM notes slow wilt may show no definite colour change.

immediate_actions.text: No treatment is indicated by this result. Continue routine checks.

non_chemical.text: Healthy suckers, drainage, balanced nutrition based on soil tests, weed control and weekly monitoring are the NIPHM-recommended foundations.

chemical_control.message: A healthy result does not call for pesticide use.

prevention.text: Check for ants and mealybug colonies at plant bases and on roots; keep field and borders free of weeds that host mealybugs.

monitoring.text: Weekly scouting; check roots and stem base of plants that look weak.

seek_expert_help: Plant looks unhealthy despite a healthy result.

classes.explanation: Mealybug wilt is associated with viruses carried by mealybugs, not a simple fungal infection. The leaf pattern is not specific, and the mealybugs may be on roots or hidden at the plant base, so absence of visible insects proves nothing.

symptoms.text: Early reddening of leaves about halfway up the plant, then pink, loss of stiffness, downward-rolling margins and dead leaf tips; roots collapse; fruit is smaller.
Slow wilt may show no colour change; quick wilt shows yellow or red leaves under heavy infestation.
Younger plants may show symptoms 2-3 months after mealybug feeding; older plants up to about 12 months.
Symptoms are most obvious in winter when growth is slow.

look_alikes.text: Phytophthora root rot, nematodes and low soil oxygen cause similar above-ground symptoms that are not diagnostic.
Nutrient deficiencies can colour leaves yellow, purple or red.

immediate_actions.text: Check roots, the base of leaves and the stem for pinkish cottony mealybugs and for ants tending them.
If under 3% of plants show wilt, remove infected plants by hand and destroy them.
If over 10% show wilt, do not use the field as a source of planting material; eradicate badly affected areas right after harvest.

non_chemical.text: Use planting material from wilt-free fields or fields with little wilt.
Destroy ant colonies and remove weeds and trash that shelter ants and mealybugs; remove alternate hosts such as hibiscus, custard apple and guava in and around the field.
After an infested crop, clear and burn plant residues before replanting; use sterilised tools in uninfested fields.
Conserve natural enemies (parasitoids, ladybird and lacewing predators); biological sprays are listed but check product label claims.

chemical_control.message: No verified chemical-control recommendation is available in the current knowledge base for this crop, condition, and location. Consult a qualified agricultural extension officer before applying pesticides.
chemical_control.reason: NIPHM says insecticides are a last resort and to follow label claims. A Kerala page names an insecticide, and a National Horticulture Board page names older products that appear obsolete. None was verified as currently registered for pineapple mealybug in India, and no doses are stored.

prevention.text: Vegetative planting material is a major route for the viruses; the disease is probably introduced in material that looks normal.
Ants tend mealybugs and raise virus spread rates in experiments.

spread_reduction.text: Ants move mealybugs between plants; wind also disperses them. Control ants, keep borders weed-free, and do not move plants from affected plots.
Both the pink mealybug (Dysmicoccus brevipes) and grey mealybug (D. neobrevipes) can acquire and transmit the virus.

vectors.text: D. brevipes is the main vector named in NIPHM; D. neobrevipes also transmits in Hawaiian experiments.

monitoring.text: Count mealybug nymphs and adults on five leaves per plant, scouting weekly after establishment.

seek_expert_help: More than a few plants affected.
Before keeping planting material from a wilt-affected field.
classes.geographic_applicability: NIPHM national package; global literature from Hawaii, Peru, Indonesia, Reunion. Not Manipur-specific.
unresolved: Hot-water treatment of planting material (Indonesian thesis) is not validated for farm use and is not in the advice.
Banana trap-crop result is early-stage and not recommended.
The role of each PMWaV species is debated; PMWaV-2 is the one associated with wilt in some studies.
Wilt may occur with few visible mealybugs.
